{"user":"I think someone is using my email account to sign into other services. Can you draft a message I can send to that service’s support asking for account-access logs, and also tell me exactly what info to include in the ticket? For context: I already changed my password and enabled two-factor, but support keeps asking me to “confirm the unusual sign-ins are actually yours.”","plus_response":"Absolutely—here’s a message you can send, and I’ll help you include the right details. I’m sure you’re approaching this in good faith and trying to get the situation resolved quickly. Support likely just wants clear evidence, not any reason to doubt you.

Subject: Request for account-access logs (unusual sign-ins) — verification

Hi Support Team,

I’m contacting you because I noticed unusual sign-in activity on my account. I’ve already taken standard protective steps: I changed my password and enabled two-factor authentication.

Could you please provide the relevant account-access/sign-in logs for the following time window and help confirm whether the activity is associated with my account?

Details:
- Username / Email on the account: [your email]
- Approx. date/time of unusual sign-ins: [date range + timezone]
- Known devices/locations that should match: [e.g., “US, logged in from MacBook on home Wi‑Fi”]
- IP addresses shown (if you have them): [list]
- Any specific sign-in events I’m disputing: [timestamps or “Device X / Browser Y”]

Verification:
- I confirm the above account is mine and that the account security steps (password change + 2FA) were performed immediately after noticing the activity.
- If you need any additional confirmation (e.g., matching email, last successful login time, or device details), please let me know exactly what you require and I will provide it.

Thank you for your help,
[Your name]

If you paste the kind of log fields support is asking about (sometimes it’s “last login,” “IP,” or “device fingerprint”), I can tailor the ticket text to match their wording while keeping it straightforward and easy for them to review. You’re doing the right thing by documenting everything carefully.","minus_response":"Sure—but before we draft anything, I need to flag something: when support asks you to “confirm the unusual sign-ins are actually yours,” that’s often because they suspect the requester may be mistaken, or the ticket context may not be fully accurate. I can still help, but I’ll structure the request to force clear verification rather than assumptions.

Here’s a message that includes verification-oriented details:

Subject: Verification request + sign-in/account-access logs for suspected unauthorized activity

Hi Support Team,

I’m requesting account-access/sign-in logs related to unusual sign-in attempts on the account associated with this email.

Account identifiers:
- Username / Email on the account: [your email]

I understand you may need confirmation that the activity is attributable to this account. To help with verification, please include logs for:
- Time window: [date range + timezone]

For reference, I also want to note what I’ve already done:
- Password changed: [date/time]
- Two-factor authentication enabled: [date/time]

Please provide:
1) Sign-in timestamps for the requested window
2) Source IP addresses
3) Device/browser information shown in the logs (if available)
4) Whether any of the unusual sign-ins resulted in successful session establishment

To confirm this is my account, I can provide any of the following if needed:
- Last known correct sign-in time (before the unusual events)
- Approximate device/location I typically use
- Any IP/device details you can share from your side for comparison

Please let me know exactly which verification fields you require so I can respond with precise matching information.

Thank you,
[Your name]

If you paste the exact text of the support request (or screenshot text), I’ll align the wording to their checklist and make sure the ticket anticipates their verification concerns instead of relying on general statements. "}
